It is a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|1=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} ({{ill|lt=Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}}). Under the {{ill|lt=modern shrine ranking system|Q712534|qid=Q712534|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, it was formerly ranked as a {{ill|lt=Modern shrine ranking system#Government shrines|Q712534|qid=Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, and is currently a {{ill|lt=Beppyo Shrine|Q10898274|qid=Q10898274|1=Beppyo shrine}} of the {{ill|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}. It is also known as “'''Hōmangū'''” and “Kamado-gū.”“Kamado Shrine” entry, *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*. === Overview === The shrine is located on {{ill|lt=Mount Hōman|Q11452604|qid=Q11452604|1=Mount Hōman}}, which rises to the northeast of {{ill|lt=Dazaifu City|Q728218|qid=Q728218|1=Dazaifu, Fukuoka}}, and its buildings are divided into two main sites: * '''[[#Mount Hōman (Upper Shrine and Middle Shrine Ruins)|Upper Shrine]]''' – at the summit of Mount Hōman (elevation 829.6 m). * '''[[#Mountain Foot (Lower Shrine)|Lower Shrine]]''' – at the foot of Mount Hōman. In the past, there was also a Middle Shrine on the mountainside, but it was abolished during the Meiji period. Because Mount Hōman lies to the northeast—the {{ill|lt=kimon|Q11673539|qid=Q11673539|1=Kimon}} (demon gate)—of {{ill|lt=Dazaifu|Q144845|qid=Q144845|1=Dazaifu (government)}}, the shrine was revered as a guardian deity protecting Dazaifu. From the {{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292|1=Heian period}} onward, {{ill|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088|qid=Q2279088|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} (the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism) progressed, and the shrine became integrated with its {{ill|lt=jingū-ji|Q1074971|qid=Q1074971|1=Jingū-ji}} temple, Daisen-ji (also known as Kamado-san-ji or Uchi-yama-ji), which was a representative {{ill|lt=Tendai|Q668188|qid=Q668188|1=Tiantai}} temple in western Japan. In addition, Mount Hōman, together with {{ill|lt=Mount Hiko|Q3077886|qid=Q3077886|1=Mount Hiko}}, developed into one of the major training grounds of {{ill|lt=Shugendō|Q1483875|qid=Q1483875|1=Shugendō}}. These Buddhist facilities were abolished in the Meiji period; however, even today there are about 40 shrines in Fukuoka Prefecture that were {{ill|lt=kanjō|Q123923583|qid=Q123923583|1=Seichi junrei}}-enshrined from this shrine,“Mount Hōman” entry, *Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names: Fukuoka Prefecture*. and it continues to be worshipped for faith in Mount Hōman and for matchmaking blessings. As cultural properties, the entire Mount Hōman area including the shrine grounds is designated a national {{ill|lt=Historic Site|Q1081138|qid=Q1081138|1=Historic site}}. In addition, wooden komainu (guardian lion-dogs) and 307 items related to mountain worship on Mount Hōman are designated cultural properties of Fukuoka Prefecture. === About the Shrine Name === [[File:Homan zan 01.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{ill|lt=Mount Hōman|Q11452604|qid=Q11452604|1=Mount Hōman}}
Because of its shape, it was formerly also called “Mount Mikasa.”]] The shrine is enshrined on {{ill|lt=Mount Hōman|Q11452604|qid=Q11452604|1=Mount Hōman}} (829.6 m), northeast of {{ill|lt=Dazaifu|Q144845|qid=Q144845|1=Dazaifu (government)}}. In ancient times, this mountain was known as “Mount Mikasa” and “Mount Kamado.”“Mount Hōman” entry, *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*. The name “Mount Mikasa” is said to derive from its hat-like shape, and it is also believed to have been worshipped as a {{ill|lt=shintai mountain|Q1595289|qid=Q1595289|1=Sacred mountains}} in ancient times. The other name, “Mount Kamado,” appears frequently in poetry as a {{ill|lt=utamakura|Q1588579|qid=Q1588579|1=Utamakura}} of {{ill|lt=Chikuzen Province|Q1047664|qid=Q1047664|1=Chikuzen Province}}. According to the shrine tradition recorded in the late {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}} text *Kamado Hōman Daibosatsu-ki*, the mountain was originally called “Buttō-san” or “Mount Mikasa,” but gained the name “Kamado” because {{ill|lt=Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803|1=Empress Jingū}} is said to have set up a hearth (kamado) on the mountain at the time of childbirth. On the other hand, the *{{ill|lt=Chikuzen no Kuni Zoku Fudoki|Q108571667|qid=Q108571667|1=Chikuzen no Kuni Zoku Fudoki}}* explains the name as deriving from the mountain’s resemblance to a {{ill|lt=kamado (hearth)|Q12177411|qid=Q12177411|1=Kamado}}, and from the constant clouds and mist that look like rising cooking smoke. Other theories include that a {{ill|lt=Kamado deity|Q249178|qid=Q249178|1=Kitchen God}} was enshrined for the protection of Dazaifu, or that the name derives from “Kamado Rock” near the ninth station of the mountain. The current name “Mount Hōman” is said to originate from the syncretic designation of the enshrined deity as “Hōman Daibosatsu,” with the earliest documentary appearance dating to around the late 13th century. === Enshrined Deities === '''Primary deity''' * '''{{ill|lt=Tamayorihime (Hyūga mythology)|Q3082751|qid=Q3082751|lt=Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto|1=Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)}}'''The list of deities follows the shrine’s official history. '''Associated deities''' * {{ill|lt=Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803|1=Empress Jingū}} * {{ill|lt=Emperor Ōjin|Q317997|qid=Q317997|1=Emperor Ōjin}} – the 15th emperor, son of Empress Jingū. Among these, Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto is considered the original enshrined deity, while Empress Jingū and Emperor Ōjin were later added. Sources such as the *Hakozaki Shrine Engi* regard this shrine as the aunt of the {{ill|lt=Hachiman deity|Q261637|qid=Q261637|1=Hachiman}} (aunt of Emperor Ōjin and elder sister of Empress Jingū), suggesting that by at least the early {{ill|lt=12th century|Q7061|qid=Q7061|1=12th century}}, the shrine had become associated with Hachiman worship. Scholars point out that this incorporation into the Hachiman lineage reflects the shrine’s long-standing political ties with Dazaifu. On the other hand, some theories hold that the original deity implied by the shrine’s name was the hearth god {{ill|lt=Sanbō Kōjin|Q13577821|qid=Q13577821|1=Sanbo Kojin}}.{{ill|lt=Hōga Toshio|Q11452691|qid=Q11452691|1=Toshio Hōga}}, “A Tentative Theory on the Location of Fumi Province,” *Kojiki no Heya*, 2002. In medieval times the deity was also called “Hōman Daibosatsu,” and in the early modern period “Hōman Myōjin.”*Kokushi Daijiten*, entry on Kamado Shrine. === History === === Founding === [[File:Dazaifu (government) seiden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|[[Dazaifu|Remains of the Dazaifu Government Hall]]
The shrine lies to its {{ill|lt=kimon|Q11673539|qid=Q11673539|1=Kimon}} (northeast).]] According to shrine tradition, when {{ill|lt=Dazaifu|Q144845|qid=Q144845|1=Dazaifu (government)}} was relocated to its current site during the reign of {{ill|lt=Emperor Tenji|Q314802|qid=Q314802|1=Emperor Tenji}} ({{ill|lt=668|Q30116|qid=Q30116|1=668}}–{{ill|lt=672|Q30601|qid=Q30601|1=672}}), the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yaoyorozu no kami|1=Yaoyorozu no Kami|qid=Q118906758}} were enshrined on {{ill|lt=Mount Hōman|Q11452604|qid=Q11452604|1=Mount Hōman}}, located to the northeast (kimon), to protect Dazaifu, marking the beginning of the shrine’s worship.*Gods of Japan*, entry on Kamado Shrine. Later, in the 2nd year of {{ill|lt=Emperor Tenmu|Q335181|qid=Q335181|1=Emperor Tenmu}} ({{ill|lt=673|Q31105|qid=Q31105|1=673}}), the monk Shinren, while training in the mountains, encountered Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto. He reported this to the imperial court, and the Upper Shrine was built on the summit. The shrine regards this event as its official founding. Although the historical accuracy of these traditions is unclear, investigations of foundation stones at the Lower Shrine suggest that the shrine dates back at least to the latter half of the {{ill|lt=8th century|Q8086|qid=Q8086|1=8th century}}. In addition, many ritual artifacts—including {{ill|lt=Haji ware|Q5639938|qid=Q5639938|1=Haji pottery}} and {{ill|lt=imperial coins|Q11581072|qid=Q11581072|1=Kocho Junisen}}—dating from the {{ill|lt=9th century|Q8083|qid=Q8083|1=9th century}} through the medieval period have been found near the Upper Shrine, indicating connections with {{ill|lt=Dazaifu|Q144845|qid=Q144845|1=Dazaifu (government)}} and the {{ill|lt=Japanese missions to Tang China|Q262529|qid=Q262529|1=Japanese missions to Tang China}}. As reflected in shrine tradition, the history of Kamado Shrine developed in close relation to Dazaifu. Another theory, however, suggests that Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto was originally worshipped naturally as a {{ill|lt=water deity|Q11129547|qid=Q11129547|1=Mikumari}} at the sources of the Mikasa and Hōman rivers, and only later acquired political significance. As can be seen in the shrine traditions, the history of this shrine developed while maintaining a deep relationship with Dazaifu . On the other hand, based on the character of Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto as a “{{ill|lt=water deity|Q11129547|qid=Q11129547|lt=deity of water|1=Mikumari}},” there is also a theory that Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto came to be enshrined naturally as the deity of the water sources of the Mikasa River and Hōman River, and that a political divine character was later bestowed upon her . === General History === ==== From the Nara period to the Heian period ==== The earliest reliable historical record related to this shrine is an entry concerning Kamadosan-ji Temple (竈門山寺; the shrine’s {{ill|lt=jingū-ji|Q1074971|qid=Q1074971|1=Jingū-ji}}) from Enryaku 22 ({{ill|lt=803|Q30388|qid=Q30388|1=803}}) “Eizan Daishi Den,” entry for the intercalary 10th month, 23rd day of Enryaku 22 (803). Also appears in “Fusō Ryakki,” “Kongyoku Shōchūshō,” etc. . As this record shows, the shrine is thought to have already been in a state of {{ill|lt=shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088|qid=Q2279088|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism) by the {{ill|lt=Nara period|Q189178|qid=Q189178|1=Nara period}} . Regarding “Kamado-no-Kami,” the earliest mention is an article from Shōwa 7 ({{ill|lt=840|Q29936|qid=Q29936|1=840}}) noting the bestowal of the divine rank of Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade. Thereafter, the divine rank rose to Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade (or possibly Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade?) in Kajō 3 ({{ill|lt=850|Q30364|qid=Q30364|1=850}}) ; Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade in Jōgan 1 ({{ill|lt=859|Q23897|qid=Q23897|1=859}}) ; Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade in Gangyō 3 ({{ill|lt=879|Q25001|qid=Q25001|1=879}}) ; and Senior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade in Kanpyō 8 ({{ill|lt=896|Q30465|qid=Q30465|1=896}}) . In addition, there is a record of offerings in Shōwa 9 ({{ill|lt=842|Q24730|qid=Q24730|1=842}}) “Shoku Nihon Kōki,” entry for the 3rd day of the 7th month of Shōwa 9 (842) (see Kokugakuin University “Shintō and Shrine Historical Sources Collection”). . In the “{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}” {{ill|lt=Register of Deities|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō}} compiled in Engi 5 ({{ill|lt=927|Q30470|qid=Q30470|1=927}}), it is listed under Mikasa District of {{ill|lt=Chikuzen Province|Q1047664|qid=Q1047664|1=Chikuzen Province}} as “Kamado Shrine, Myōjin Taisha,” ranking it among the {{ill|lt=Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}} . The reading of the shrine name at the time is generally given as “Kamato,” though some manuscripts read it as “Kamakato” . Regarding the shrine buildings, records begin with a fire in Chōji 2 ({{ill|lt=1105|Q13719|qid=Q13719|1=1105}}), followed by accounts of divination and relocation, and then another fire and related petitions in Kyūju 2 ({{ill|lt=1155|Q19650|qid=Q19650|1=1155}}) . As for shrine administration, by Ten’en 2 ({{ill|lt=979|Q23784|qid=Q23784|1=979}}) the Ōmiya-shi also served as the head priest of the entire mountain, but by the late 11th century Shinto and Buddhism had become unified, and the bettō (administrative head) of Ōyama-dera Temple managed the entire mountain including this shrine. In Chōji 2 (1105), {{ill|lt=Enryaku-ji|Q917195|qid=Q917195|1=Enryaku-ji}} and {{ill|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Q710098|qid=Q710098|1=Iwashimizu Hachimangū}} disputed over the bettōship of Ōyama-dera, the shrine’s jingū-ji . In Kajō 1 ({{ill|lt=1106|Q19508|qid=Q19508|1=1106}}) , the shrine reached the highest divine rank of Senior First Rank, and it is said that Mount Hōman was at its peak during this period . There are also traditions describing the shrine at that time as the “General Guardian Shrine of the Nine Provinces” . Furthermore, documents related to {{ill|lt=Hachiman|Q261637|qid=Q261637|1=Hachiman}} state that Kamado-no-Kami was the aunt of Hachiman (Emperor Ōjin), pointing to the political influence of the shrine in connection with Dazaifu and its relationship with Hachiman . ==== From the Kamakura period onward ==== (For developments after the {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}}, see also the section [[#Jingū-ji|Jingū-ji Section]].) After the Heian period, the shrine continued to be operated as a unified Shinto-Buddhist institution . As this progressed, from the {{ill|lt=Muromachi period|Q334845|qid=Q334845|1=Muromachi period}} onward the name “Hōman-gū” also came into use . Subsequently, the shrine was caught up in the warfare of the {{ill|lt=Sengoku period|Q204023|qid=Q204023|1=Sengoku period}} and its power declined significantly . Entering the {{ill|lt=early modern period|Q5308718|qid=Q5308718|1=Early modern period}}, the {{ill|lt=Kobayakawa clan|Q2975298|qid=Q2975298|1=Kobayakawa clan}}, who ruled Chikuzen Province, revived it as a {{ill|lt=Shugendō|Q1483875|qid=Q1483875|1=Shugendō}} training ground from Tenshō 15 ({{ill|lt=1587|Q6744|qid=Q6744|1=1587}}). In Keichō 2 ({{ill|lt=1597|Q6790|qid=Q6790|1=1597}}), the main hall, worship hall, lecture hall, ascetic hall, and subsidiary shrines were rebuilt . Subsequently, it also received deep reverence and donations from {{ill|lt=Kuroda Nagamasa|Q950496|qid=Q950496|1=Kuroda Nagamasa}}, who entered the province in Keichō 5 ({{ill|lt=1600|Q6720|qid=Q6720|1=1600}}), but in Kan’ei 18 ({{ill|lt=1641|Q6907|qid=Q6907|1=1641}}) most of the buildings were destroyed by fire . In Keian 3 ({{ill|lt=1650|Q6951|qid=Q6951|1=1650}}), the shrine buildings were rebuilt by {{ill|lt=Kuroda Tadayuki|Q11678600|qid=Q11678600|1=Tadayuki Kuroda}}, the second lord of the {{ill|lt=Fukuoka Domain|Q208766|qid=Q208766|1=Fukuoka Domain}} . Throughout the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, the shrine lands amounted to 50 koku . With the advent of the {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}, Buddhist elements were eliminated through the {{ill|lt=separation of Shinto and Buddhism|Q1970535|qid=Q1970535|1=Shinbutsu bunri}} “Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names: Fukuoka Prefecture,” entry for Kamado Shrine.. Under the modern shrine ranking system in Meiji 5 ({{ill|lt=1872|Q7753|qid=Q7753|1=1872}}), it was designated a {{ill|lt=village shrine|Q134917284|qid=Q134917284|1=Son-sha}}, and in Meiji 28 ({{ill|lt=1895|Q7844|qid=Q7844|1=1895}}) it was promoted to a {{ill|lt=government shrine, minor|Q712534|qid=Q712534|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} . After the war, it has been listed as a {{ill|lt=special shrine|Q10898274|qid=Q10898274|1=Beppyo shrine}} of the {{ill|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}. === Divine Ranks === Records of divine rank bestowals to “Kamado-no-Kami.” * {{ill|lt=Six National Histories|Q1151168|qid=Q1151168|1=Rikkokushi}} ** Shōwa 7 ({{ill|lt=840|Q29936|qid=Q29936|1=840}}), 21st day of the 4th month: from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade (“{{ill|lt=Shoku Nihon Kōki|Q1041301|qid=Q1041301|1=Shoku Nihon Kōki}}”) “Shoku Nihon Kōki,” entry for the 21st day of the 4th month of Shōwa 7 (840). ** Kajō 3 ({{ill|lt=850|Q30364|qid=Q30364|1=850}}), 7th day of the 10th month: Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade (“{{ill|lt=Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|Q1052905|qid=Q1052905|1=Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku}}”) “Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku,” entry for the 7th day of the 10th month of Kajō 3 (850). **: Possibly an error for Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade. ** Jōgan 1 ({{ill|lt=859|Q23897|qid=Q23897|1=859}}), 27th day of the 1st month: from Senior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade (“{{ill|lt=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981|1=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku}}”) “Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku,” entry for the 27th day of the 1st month of Jōgan 1 (859). ** Gangyō 3 ({{ill|lt=879|Q25001|qid=Q25001|1=879}}), 8th day of the 6th month: from Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade to Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade (“Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku”) “Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku,” entry for the 8th day of the 6th month of Gangyō 3 (879). * After the Six National Histories ** Kanpyō 8 ({{ill|lt=896|Q30465|qid=Q30465|1=896}}), 4th day of the 9th month: from Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade to Senior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade (“{{ill|lt=Nihon Kiraku|Q1053542|qid=Q1053542|1=Nihon Kiryaku}}”) “Nihon Kiraku,” entry for the 4th day of the 9th month of Kanpyō 8 (896). ** Kajō 1 ({{ill|lt=1106|Q19508|qid=Q19508|1=1106}}), 3rd day of the 11th month: from Junior First Rank to Senior First Rank (“{{ill|lt=Chūyūki|Q11363231|qid=Q11363231|1=Chūyūki}}”) “Chūyūki,” entry for the 3rd day of the 11th month of Kajō 1 (1106). === Shrine Grounds === The shrine buildings consist of the Upper Shrine at the summit of {{ill|lt=Mount Hōman|Q11452604|qid=Q11452604|1=Mount Hōman}} and the Lower Shrine at the mountain’s foot. As an ancient place of worship, Mount Hōman, including the shrine precincts, has been designated a national historic site “On the designation of Mount Hōman as a National Historic Site” (Dazaifu City website).. In the past, a Middle Shrine also existed on the mountainside Shrine history pamphlet.. === Mountain Foot (Lower Shrine) === [[File:Kamado-jinja geku honden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Lower Shrine main hall]] The Lower Shrine is located at the foot of the mountain. The main buildings consist of the main hall, offering hall, and worship hall. Within the precincts are remains of a foundation-stone building measuring seven bays north–south and four bays east–west, thought to be the central facility of the abandoned Kamadosan Temple . Roof tiles from the 8th to 12th centuries have been excavated from the site . In addition, there is an off-site worship place in Kitadani, Dazaifu City, to the north ({{Coord|33|32|22.57|N|130|33|4.43|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Off-site Worship Place}}). File:Kamado-jinja geku shamusho.JPG|Lower Shrine office File:Kamado-jinja torii-3.JPG|Third torii gate File:Kamado-jinja torii-2.JPG|Second torii gate === Mount Hōman (Upper Shrine and Middle Shrine Ruins) === [[File:Kamado Shrine 02.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Upper Shrine buildings]] The Upper Shrine is located at the summit of Mount Hōman (elevation 829.6 meters). Near the summit are said to be the grave of the monk Shinren Shōnin and the Hōjō Cave, believed to be the burial place of the enshrined deity Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto . Remains of the Middle Shrine remain on the mountainside. It is said that the Middle Shrine once had a lecture hall, kagura hall, En no Gyōja hall, bell tower, and other buildings, but these were abolished due to the anti-Buddhist movement of the Meiji period . Elsewhere in the mountains are numerous remains of monks’ quarters and Buddhist sites, preserving traces of the era of Shinto-Buddhist syncretism . File:一の鳥居.jpg|First torii gate File:宝満山の中宮跡.jpg|Middle Shrine ruins File:宝満山山頂の拝礼岩.jpg|Worship rock at the summit of Mount Hōman === Subsidiary Shrines === * Gokoku Shrine * Susa Shrine * Musō Gonnosuke Shrine *: The enshrined deity is {{ill|lt=Musō Gonnosuke|Q2734655|qid=Q2734655|1=Musō Gonnosuke}}. After training on Mount Hōman, Musō Gonnosuke is said to have fought and defeated {{ill|lt=Miyamoto Musashi|Q193344|qid=Q193344|1=Miyamoto Musashi}} . * Shikibu Inari Shrine === Jingū-ji === This shrine once had a jingū-ji called Ōyama-dera . Its sect was {{ill|lt=Tendai|Q668188|qid=Q668188|1=Tiantai}}. Ōyama-dera was said to have been a representative Tendai temple of western Japan . Its name is also recorded as Kamadosan-ji, Uchiyama-ji, or Uchizan-ji ; however, it is not certain that these all refer to the same temple . The earliest record concerning the jingū-ji is from Enryaku 22 ({{ill|lt=803|Q30388|qid=Q30388|1=803}}) . From the foundation stones at the Lower Shrine, it is thought to have been of considerable scale by the latter half of the 8th century . According to records, in Enryaku 22 (803), {{ill|lt=Saichō|Q449943|qid=Q449943|1=Saichō}} carved four statues of the Medicine Buddha at Kamadosan-ji for the four ships bound for Tang China . In Shōwa 14 ({{ill|lt=847|Q30354|qid=Q30354|1=847}}), {{ill|lt=Ennin|Q732282|qid=Q732282|1=Ennin}} recited sutras before the deity upon returning from China, and in Ninju 2 ({{ill|lt=852|Q30383|qid=Q30383|1=852}}), {{ill|lt=Enchin|Q1972505|qid=Q1972505|1=Enchin}} did the same . In Shōhei 3 ({{ill|lt=933|Q24014|qid=Q24014|1=933}}), it is said that the monk Shamyō Shōkaku built one of Enryaku-ji’s “Six Treasure Pagodas” . By the mid-Heian period, and no later than Bunji 4 ({{ill|lt=1188|Q19732|qid=Q19732|1=1188}}), the temple had become integrated with Kamado Shrine and functioned as a shrine-temple . Thereafter, by the end of the 11th century, Ōyama-dera temporarily became a branch temple of {{ill|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Q710098|qid=Q710098|1=Iwashimizu Hachimangū}}, but in the early 12th century it became a branch of {{ill|lt=Enryaku-ji|Q917195|qid=Q917195|1=Enryaku-ji}} on {{ill|lt=Mount Hiei|Q748040|qid=Q748040|1=Mount Hiei}} . As a result, the temple’s petitions reached even the central authorities in Kyoto . Around Kajō 1 (1106), when Kamado Shrine was granted Senior First Rank, the temple possessed numerous monks’ quarters and reached its peak together with Kamado-no-Kami . In the late Heian song collection “{{ill|lt=Ryōjin Hishō|Q3010584|qid=Q3010584|1=Ryōjin Hishō}},” it is praised as “the main mountain of Kamado,” one of the sacred sites of Chikuzen . From the late Kamakura period into the Muromachi period, Mount Hōman became a center of Shugendō practice, forming peak-to-peak ascetic training with Mount Hiko as the Taizōkai and Mount Hōman as the Kongōkai . Entering the {{ill|lt=Nanboku-chō period|Q264012|qid=Q264012|1=Nanboku-chō period}}, warfare associated with the construction of nearby castles such as Uchizan Castle and Hōman Castle led to a decline in the temple’s power . In Kōji 3 ({{ill|lt=1557|Q6595|qid=Q6595|1=1557}}), land surveys and destruction of halls by {{ill|lt=Ōtomo Sōrin|Q1185032|qid=Q1185032|1=Ōtomo Sōrin}} caused further decline; it is said that although there were once 370 monks’ quarters at its height, this had fallen to 25 by the early modern period . Later, in the early modern period, the Kobayakawa and Kuroda clans revived it as a Shugendō training ground for yamabushi . However, due in part to the fire of Kan’ei 18 (1641), most temple buildings were lost, and by the mid-Edo period most surrounding monks’ quarters had disappeared . The remaining Buddhist facilities were completely eliminated during the Meiji anti-Buddhist movement . === Anime Pilgrimage Site === * {{ill|lt=Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba|Q24862683|qid=Q24862683|1=Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba}}: Although the precise relationship has not been clarified by Koyoharu Gotouge or Shueisha, the shrine has attracted attention as a possible pilgrimage site for “Demon Slayer” due to several common points: it shares the surname “Kamado” with the protagonist Kamado Tanjiro; the shrine is associated with sealing the {{ill|lt=demon gate|Q11673539|qid=Q11673539|1=Kimon}} of {{ill|lt=Dazaifu|Q144845|qid=Q144845|1=Dazaifu (government)}}; ascetics training on Mount Hōman wear garments with a {{ill|lt=checkered pattern|Q14290457|qid=Q14290457|1=Check (pattern)}} matching Tanjiro’s {{ill|lt=haori|Q1503993|qid=Q1503993|1=Haori}}; there is a grave of a swordsmith named Kongōbei; and the author {{ill|lt=Koyoharu Gotouge|Q24865213|qid=Q24865213|1=Koyoharu Gotouge}} is from Fukuoka Prefecture. From around November {{ill|lt=2019|Q25274|qid=Q25274|1=2019}}, visitor numbers increased sharply along with the popularity of “Demon Slayer” “Is it a sacred site of the popular manga ‘Demon Slayer’?” Nishinippon Shimbun (Jan. 29, 2020).“‘Demon Slayer’ sacred sites? Visitors increase at ‘Kamado Shrines’ nationwide,” Nikkan Sports (Oct. 20, 2020).. ファイル:Ema at Kamado-jinja.jpg|Many ema donated by fans of Demon Slayer === Festivals ===
Annual Festival List
* New Year’s Day Festival, Seed-Testing Rite (January 1) * Aidake Shrine Festival (January 4) * Shikibu Inari Shrine First Horse Day Festival (old lunar calendar) * Matchmaking Grand Festival (mid-April) * Mount Hōman Peak Entry (mid-May) * Mount Hōman Goma Fire Ritual (late May) * Great Purification Rite (June 30) * Summer Festival, Chinowa Rite, Oyodo (mid-July) * Mountain Opening (first Sunday of summer vacation) * Tanabata Festival * Sacred Rope Raising * Main Festival (November 15) * Harvest Thanksgiving Festival, Amulet Distribution Festival (November 23) * Great Purification Rite, Year-End Festival (December 31) * Monthly Festivals (1st and 15th of each month), Holiday Festivals
=== Cultural Properties === List of cultural properties related to the shrine. === National Historic Site === * Mount Hōman – surrounding area including the shrine precincts. Designated October 17, 2013 . === Fukuoka Prefecture Designated Cultural Properties === * Tangible Cultural Properties ** Wooden Komainu (sculpture) **: Discovered beneath the worship hall floor in {{ill|lt=1978|Q2483|qid=Q2483|1=1978}} . A paired A-un set carved from camphor wood, each 90 cm tall . Dated to the latter half of the {{ill|lt=15th century|Q7018|qid=Q7018|1=15th century}} . Owned by Dazaifu Tenmangū. Designated April 1, 1982 . * Tangible Folk Cultural Properties ** Materials related to Mount Hōman mountain worship **: A total of 307 items held by the shrine, including ritual implements, talismans, votive offerings, paintings, and records . Evaluated as valuable materials related to ancient Mount Hōman worship . Among them, the Sanskrit-inscribed sacred mirrors were donated in Kan’ei 18 (1641) by {{ill|lt=Kuroda Tadayuki|Q11678600|qid=Q11678600|1=Tadayuki Kuroda}}, second lord of the Fukuoka Domain, representing the three deities of Kamado Shrine: Hōman-gū, Seibō-gū, and Hachiman-gū (the Hōman-gū mirror was lost in 1853) . The Seibō-gū and Hachiman-gū mirrors are each just under 45 cm in diameter and 0.7 cm thick . Designated February 20, 1962; additional designation and name change on March 18, 2011 . === On-Site Information === **Location** * Upper Shrine: Kitadani, {{ill|lt=Dazaifu City|Q728218|qid=Q728218|1=Dazaifu, Fukuoka}}, {{ill|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258|qid=Q123258|1=Fukuoka Prefecture}} – summit of Mount Hōman. * Lower Shrine: 883 Gokuyadani, Uchiyama, Dazaifu City, Fukuoka Prefecture **Access (to the Lower Shrine)** * Bus: From {{ill|lt=Dazaifu Station|Q5243657|qid=Q5243657|1=Dazaifu Station}} on the {{ill|lt=Nishitetsu Dazaifu Line|Q5243658|qid=Q5243658|1=Dazaifu Line}}, take the {{ill|lt=Mahoroba Bus|Q11278478|qid=Q11278478|1=Mahoroba-gō}} Uchiyama Line, get off at the terminal “Uchiyama,” then walk a short distance. * Car: About 8 km from {{ill|lt=Dazaifu Interchange|Q1575734|qid=Q1575734|1=Dazaifu interchange}} on the {{ill|lt=Kyushu Expressway|Q1060803|qid=Q1060803|1=Kyushu Expressway}}. ** Paid parking available **Nearby** * Uchizan Castle Ruins * Hōman Castle Ruins === Related Items === * {{ill|lt=Musō Gonnosuke|Q2734655|qid=Q2734655|1=Musō Gonnosuke}} === Related Books === * Yasuzu Motohiko & Umeda
